title: Complement system
covers: How complement is activated by the classical, lectin and alternative pathways, what its fragments do, how it is regulated, and the diseases of complement deficiency.

items.p: A group of plasma proteins made by the liver. Most are inactive enzymes (zymogens) that cut and activate one another in a cascade.
Complement belongs to innate immunity: it works even without antibodies. It kills pathogens in three ways.

ul: Opsonization and phagocytosis (C3b)
Inflammation (C3a, C4a, C5a)
Lysis by the membrane attack complex (C5b to C9)

items.p: Names follow the order of discovery, not the order of reaction: C1, C4, C2, C3, C5.
Every pathway ends in a C3 convertase that cleaves C3.

ul: C3a: small peptide, inflammation
C3b: the main effector molecule; binds covalently to the microbe

items.p: Activation stays on the pathogen surface. C4b or C3b that fails to bind is hydrolyzed and inactivated.

table: C1q binds the pathogen or antibody (IgG, IgM) on it
MBL or ficolins bind sugars such as mannose
Spontaneous C3 hydrolysis (tickover), or C3b from other pathways

items.p: The classical convertase is written C4b2b in new texts and C4b2a in older ones.
C1 is the sensor: C1q (recognition, a hexamer of trimers) with the proteases C1r and C1s (a calcium-dependent tetramer).

ul: C1q binds, C1r activates itself, C1r cleaves C1s
C1s cleaves C4, then C2
C4b plus C2b form the C3 convertase

items.p: Mannose-binding lectin (a collectin made in the liver) and three ficolins circulate as pattern recognition receptors.

ul: MBL: low affinity but high avidity for repeated sugars; rises in the acute-phase response
MBL carries MASP proteases. MASP-2 cleaves C4 and C2, like C1s.
Ficolins bind acetylated sugars and are more abundant than MBL

items.p: It needs no early components. It runs at a low level all the time and amplifies the other pathways.

ul: C3b binds factor B; factor D cleaves factor B; result: C3bBb
Properdin (factor P) stabilizes C3bBb. It is the only positive regulator and comes from neutrophil granules.
C3bBb plus another C3b is the C5 convertase

items.p: C5 convertase splits C5. C5a is strongly inflammatory. C5b starts the membrane attack complex.
C9 polymerizes into a pore. Water and ions enter, and the cell swells and bursts. The MAC matters most against Neisseria.
Healthy host cells carry regulators; infected cells lose them.

table: Removes C1r and C1s from C1q
Cofactor for factor I, which cleaves C3b and C4b
Stops C9 joining C5b-8: no MAC

items.p: Most complement deficiencies are autosomal recessive. Two exceptions: properdin deficiency is X-linked recessive, and C1 inhibitor deficiency is autosomal dominant.

ul: MBL or MASP-2 deficiency: respiratory infections in early childhood
Properdin deficiency: Neisseria meningitidis
Early components (C1 to C4): pyogenic infections and lupus, from poor clearance of immune complexes
Terminal components (C5 to C9): recurrent Neisseria infections
C1 inhibitor deficiency: hereditary angioedema. Swelling of skin, gut and larynx. Treat with recombinant C1 inhibitor.
DAF deficiency from an acquired stem-cell mutation: paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. Hemolysis, thrombosis, marrow failure, dark morning urine.

items.p: Tests: CH50 (or CH100) for overall activity, and C3 and C4 levels.

items.note: The slide dates the discovery of complement by Jules Bordet to the "1980s". The historical date is the 1890s.
The slide attributes angioedema to "C2 kinin, a bradykinin". Standard sources name bradykinin from the kallikrein pathway as the main mediator. Use the slide wording for the exam.

cards.q: The three effector functions of complement, and the fragment for each
cards.a: Opsonization: C3b. Inflammation: C3a, C4a, C5a. Lysis: MAC (C5b–C9).

cards.q: What is the critical step of complement activation?
cards.a: A C3 convertase cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b.

cards.q: C3 convertase of the classical and lectin pathways
cards.a: C4b2b (older texts: C4b2a)

cards.q: C3 convertase of the alternative pathway
cards.a: C3bBb (stabilized by properdin)

cards.q: What does the C1 complex contain?
cards.a: C1q (recognition protein, hexamer of trimers) plus proteases C1r and C1s

cards.q: Order of events after C1q binds
cards.a: C1r autoactivates, cleaves C1s; C1s cleaves C4 then C2.

cards.q: Which protease of the lectin pathway cleaves C4 and C2?
cards.a: MASP-2

cards.q: What triggers the lectin pathway?
cards.a: Mannose-binding lectin or one of three ficolins binding microbial sugars

cards.q: Two ways the alternative pathway starts
cards.a: Tickover (spontaneous hydrolysis of C3) and C3b supplied by the other pathways (amplification loop)

cards.q: Which enzyme cleaves factor B?
cards.a: Factor D

cards.q: The only positive regulator of complement
cards.a: Properdin (factor P), from neutrophil secondary granules

cards.q: Alternative-pathway C5 convertase
cards.a: C3bBbC3b

cards.q: What forms the pore of the MAC?
cards.a: Polymerized C9, at the site where C5b bound

cards.q: What does C1 inhibitor do?
cards.a: Dissociates activated C1r and C1s from C1q

cards.q: What does DAF do?
cards.a: Accelerates decay of the C3 convertases

cards.q: What does CD59 do?
cards.a: Blocks C9 from joining C5b-8, preventing the MAC

cards.q: What does MCP do?
cards.a: Cofactor for factor I in cleaving C3b (and C4b)

cards.q: Inheritance exceptions among complement deficiencies
cards.a: Properdin: X-linked recessive. C1 inhibitor: autosomal dominant. The rest: autosomal recessive.

cards.q: Properdin deficiency or C5–C9 deficiency predisposes to...
cards.a: Neisseria infections (meningitis, gonorrhea)

cards.q: Why do early classical deficiencies (C1q, C2, C4) cause lupus?
cards.a: Immune complexes are not cleared.

cards.q: Hereditary angioedema: defect and treatment
cards.a: C1 inhibitor deficiency (autosomal dominant); recombinant C1 inhibitor

cards.q: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria: mechanism
cards.a: Acquired stem-cell mutation, loss of DAF, uncontrolled complement on red cells

cards.q: Three features of PNH
cards.a: Hemolytic anemia (dark morning urine), thrombosis, impaired bone marrow function

cards.q: Screening test for overall complement activity
cards.a: CH50 (or CH100), plus C3 and C4 levels

questions.stem: Complement was first described as a heat-labile plasma substance that "complements" the bactericidal activity of immune sera. Which statement reflects how the lecture positions it today?

options.A: An adaptive mechanism that protects against infection once specific antibodies have been produced
options.B: An essential innate mechanism that protects against infection even in the absence of antibodies
options.C: A heat-stable effector of cellular immunity that requires priming by antigen-presenting cells
options.D: An innate mechanism restricted to the classical pathway and dependent on immune sera
options.E: A humoral mechanism whose components are synthesized by plasma cells after antigen exposure

questions.explanation: Complement was discovered through the classical pathway as an effector of the humoral response, but it is an essential mechanism of innate immunity that provides protection in the absence of antibodies. A: It was first seen that way (classical pathway), but it is an essential innate mechanism working without antibodies. C: It is heat-labile and needs no priming. D: Lectin and alternative pathways work without antibody. E: Complement proteins are synthesized by the liver.

questions.stem: The final outcome of complement activation is killing the pathogen through three effector mechanisms. Which set is correct?

options.A: Membrane attack, phagocytosis and antibody production
options.B: Phagocytosis, inflammation and NK-mediated killing
options.C: Membrane attack, inflammation and clonal expansion
options.D: Opsonization, antigen presentation and membrane attack
options.E: Membrane attack, phagocytosis and inflammation

questions.explanation: Complement kills directly (membrane attack), by facilitating phagocytosis, and by inducing inflammatory responses. A: Antibody production is not a complement effector mechanism. B: NK killing is a separate innate mechanism. C: Clonal expansion belongs to adaptive immunity. D: Antigen presentation is not listed as a complement effector mechanism.

questions.stem: Which statement about complement proteases is correct?

options.A: They are produced as inactive zymogens and become active after proteolytic cleavage, usually by another complement protein
options.B: They are produced as active enzymes and are switched off by proteolytic cleavage, usually by another complement protein
options.C: They are produced as inactive zymogens and become active after phosphorylation by membrane kinases
options.D: They are produced as inactive zymogens and become active after binding calcium in the plasma, without cleavage
options.E: They are produced by neutrophils as active enzymes stored in secondary granules until release

questions.explanation: Complement proteases are inactive pro-enzymes (zymogens) that become enzymatically active only after proteolytic cleavage, usually by another complement protein, giving a tightly regulated cascade. B: They are made inactive and activated by cleavage. C: Activation is by proteolytic cleavage. D: Cleavage is required for activation. E: Storage in neutrophil secondary granules is described for properdin.

questions.stem: Which complement receptors are listed in the lecture?

options.A: CR1, CR2, CR3 and CR5
options.B: CR1, CR2 and CD59
options.C: CR1, CR2, CR3 and CR4
options.D: CR1, DAF, MCP and CR4
options.E: C3aR, C5aR, CR1 and MBL

questions.explanation: The slide lists complement receptors CR1, CR2, CR3 and CR4. A: CR5 is not listed. B: CD59 is a regulator that blocks MAC formation. D: DAF and MCP are regulators. E: MBL is a soluble pattern recognition receptor of the lectin pathway.

questions.stem: Why does C4 act before C2 and C3 in the classical pathway even though its number is higher?

options.A: Complement proteins are named by molecular weight, not by the sequence of reactions
options.B: Complement proteins are named by plasma concentration, from most to least abundant
options.C: C4 belongs to the alternative pathway, which was discovered before the classical pathway
options.D: Complement proteins are named by order of discovery, not by the sequence of reactions
options.E: C4 is a cleavage product of C1 and is renumbered after cleavage

questions.explanation: The names depend on order of discovery rather than the reaction sequence (C1, C4, C2, C3, C5…). A: Naming follows order of discovery. B: Naming follows order of discovery. C: The classical pathway was discovered first and C4 belongs to it. E: C4 is cleaved by C1s; it is not a product of C1.

questions.stem: Regarding complement nomenclature, which statement is correct?

options.A: The classical C3 convertase is now written C4b2b; older literature called it C4b2a
options.B: The classical C3 convertase is now written C4b2a; older literature called it C4b2b
options.C: The classical C3 convertase is written C3bBb in both old and new literature
options.D: The classical C3 convertase is now written C4a2a because the small fragments stay bound
options.E: The classical C3 convertase is now written C1s4b; C2 was dropped from the name

questions.explanation: C2 was the exception to the suffix rule (C2a used to denote the larger fragment); this was rectified, so the convertase is C4b2b (previously C4b2a). B: It is the other way round. C: C3bBb is the alternative pathway convertase. D: C4a is released as an inflammatory mediator. E: C2b remains part of the convertase.

questions.stem: Which statement about C1q, C1r and C1s is correct?

options.A: They are the cleavage products of C1, named in order of size
options.B: They are alternative pathway proteins named with lowercase letters
options.C: They are the three fragments released when C1 inhibitor acts
options.D: They are isoforms of C1 synthesized by different tissues
options.E: They are not cleavage products; together they constitute C1

questions.explanation: Lowercase suffixes normally mark cleavage products (C3a, C3b), but C1q, C1r and C1s are not cleavage products: they all constitute C1. A: They are an exception to the suffix rule. B: Alternative pathway proteins take capital letters such as factor B and factor D. C: C1 inhibitor dissociates C1r and C1s from C1q but does not generate them by cleavage. D: They are subunits of a single complex.

questions.stem: Proteins of the alternative pathway were discovered later. How are they and their cleavage products designated?

options.A: Capital letters such as factor B and factor D; products B1 and B2
options.B: Numbers such as C6 and C7; products C6a and C6b
options.C: Capital letters such as factor B and factor D; products Ba and Bb
options.D: Lowercase letters such as factor b and factor d; products BA and BB
options.E: Capital letters such as factor P and factor H; products Pa and Hb

questions.explanation: Alternative pathway proteins are designated by capital letters (factor B, factor D); their cleavage products are Ba, Bb, Da, Db. A: Products take lowercase letter suffixes. B: Those are terminal components. D: Factors are capital letters; fragments take lowercase suffixes. E: The examples and products given on the slide are factors B and D, with Ba, Bb.

questions.stem: What is the critical step in complement activation, and which product is the main effector molecule?

options.A: C3 convertase cleaves C3; C3a is the main effector molecule
options.B: C5 convertase cleaves C5; C5b is the main effector molecule
options.C: C1s cleaves C4; C4b is the main effector molecule
options.D: C3 convertase cleaves C3; C3b is the main effector molecule
options.E: Factor D cleaves factor B; Bb is the main effector molecule

questions.explanation: The critical step is cleavage of C3 by a C3 convertase. C3a is a small peptide that binds specific receptors and helps induce inflammation; C3b is the main effector molecule. A: C3a is the small peptide that helps induce inflammation. B: The critical step is cleavage of C3. C: C4 cleavage is an early classical step. E: This forms the alternative convertase but is not the critical step named.

questions.stem: Why does C3 activation by the lectin and classical pathways occur on the pathogen and not in plasma or on host cells?

options.A: Both pathways are initiated by spontaneous hydrolysis of C3, and the product diffuses to the pathogen
options.B: Both are initiated by proteins that bind pathogen surfaces, and activating events stay confined to that site
options.C: Both pathways need antibody, which is found on pathogens and not on host cells
options.D: Both pathways are initiated by properdin, which binds pathogen membranes
options.E: Both pathways are initiated in plasma, and the C3 convertase is then carried to the pathogen by C1 inhibitor

questions.explanation: Lectin and classical pathways are initiated by proteins binding the surface of pathogens; activating events are confined to this same site, so C3 activation also occurs there. A: Spontaneous hydrolysis (tickover) belongs to the alternative pathway. C: The lectin pathway needs no antibody. D: Properdin stabilizes the alternative convertase. E: Initiation is on the pathogen surface.

questions.stem: Which description of the C1 complex is correct?

options.A: C1q, a hexamer of trimers, is the recognition protein; C1r and C1s form a Ca2+-dependent C1s-C1r-C1r-C1s tetramer
options.B: C1q, a trimer of hexamers, is the protease; C1r and C1s form a Mg2+-dependent recognition tetramer
options.C: C1s, a hexamer of trimers, is the recognition protein; C1q and C1r form a Ca2+-dependent tetramer
options.D: C1q, a hexamer of trimers, is the recognition protein; C1r and C1s bind it covalently as a single C1r-C1s heterodimer
options.E: C1q, a pentamer of dimers, is the recognition protein; C1r and C1s form a Ca2+-independent tetramer

questions.explanation: C1 comprises the recognition protein C1q (hexamer of trimers) with proteases C1r and C1s, which interact non-covalently into a Ca2+-dependent C1s-C1r-C1r-C1s tetramer that folds into the arms of C1q. B: C1q is a hexamer of trimers and the recognition protein; the tetramer is calcium-dependent. C: The recognition protein is C1q. D: C1r and C1s interact non-covalently as a tetramer (C1r2s2). E: C1q is a hexamer of trimers and assembly is calcium-dependent.

questions.stem: After C1q binds its target, what is the order of events?

options.A: C1s autoactivates, C1s cleaves C1r, C1r cleaves C4 and then C2
options.B: C1r autoactivates, C1r cleaves C1s, C1s cleaves C2 and then C4
options.C: C1r autoactivates, C1r cleaves C1s, C1s cleaves C4 and then C2
options.D: C1r autoactivates, C1r cleaves C4, C1s cleaves C2
options.E: C1q cleaves C1r, C1r cleaves C1s, C1s cleaves C3 directly

questions.explanation: Recognition by C1q leads to autoactivation of C1r, which cleaves C1s; C1s cleaves C4, C4b binds C2, and C1s cleaves C2 to give C4b2b. A: C1r is activated first and cleaves C1s. B: C4 is cleaved first; C4b then binds C2. D: C1s cleaves both C4 and C2. E: C1q is a recognition protein, and C3 is cleaved by the convertase.

questions.stem: C1q can start the classical pathway in two ways. Which pair is correct, and which part of C1q is shown beside its collagen-like domain?

options.A: Binding directly to pathogen surfaces or to mannose residues; lectin domains
options.B: Binding to antibody bound to pathogens or to free antibody in plasma; globular heads
options.C: Binding to C3b on pathogens or to antibody bound to pathogens; thioester domains
options.D: Binding directly to pathogen surfaces or to antibody bound to pathogens; globular heads
options.E: Binding directly to host cell surfaces or to immune sera; serine protease domains

questions.explanation: C1q binds directly to pathogen surfaces or indirectly to antibody bound to pathogens. The figure labels its globular heads and collagen-like domain. A: Mannose recognition belongs to MBL. B: Free antibody is not described as an activator. C: C3b-driven activation is the alternative amplification loop. E: Activation is on pathogens, and proteases are C1r and C1s.

questions.stem: Antibodies bound to a soluble antigen circulate in plasma. What does the lecture say about classical pathway activation in this setting?

options.A: Activation is stronger than on a pathogen surface
options.B: Activation proceeds through MASP-2 instead of C1s
options.C: Activation needs a single antibody regardless of antibody type
options.D: Activation occurs but C4b is not cleaved
options.E: Activation is physically hard to occur

questions.explanation: Depending on the antibody type, one or several antibodies are needed for activation; if antibodies are bound to soluble antigens, activation is physically hard to occur. A: The slide states the opposite. B: MASP-2 belongs to the lectin pathway. C: The number needed depends on antibody type, and soluble antigen makes activation hard. D: Not what is stated.

questions.stem: In the classical pathway, what happens to the two fragments produced when C1s cleaves C4?

options.A: C4b acts as a mediator of inflammation; C4a binds covalently to the pathogen surface and then binds C2
options.B: C4a acts as a mediator of inflammation; C4b binds covalently to the pathogen surface and then binds C2
options.C: C4a acts as an opsonin for phagocytes; C4b binds C1q and dissociates C1r and C1s
options.D: C4a binds factor B; C4b is cleaved by factor D into the C3 convertase
options.E: C4a polymerizes into a membrane pore; C4b is released into plasma as an anaphylatoxin

questions.explanation: C1s cleaves C4 into C4a (mediator of inflammation) and C4b, which binds covalently to the pathogen surface, binds C2, and after C1s cleaves C2 forms C4b2b. A: The roles are reversed. C: Dissociation of C1r/C1s is the action of C1 inhibitor. D: Factors B and D belong to the alternative pathway. E: Pore formation is by C9, and C4b stays on the surface.

questions.stem: What happens to C4b that fails to bond rapidly with a pathogen membrane?

options.A: Its thioester bond is hydrolyzed and C4b becomes a soluble C3 convertase
options.B: It binds C2 in plasma and activates C3 in the fluid phase
options.C: It is stabilized by properdin until a pathogen is met
options.D: It is recycled into intact C4 by C1 inhibitor
options.E: Its thioester bond is hydrolyzed and C4b is irreversibly inactivated

questions.explanation: If C4b does not rapidly form the bond with a pathogen membrane, the thioester bond is cleaved by hydrolysis and C4b is irreversibly inactivated. A: Hydrolysis inactivates it. B: Activation is confined to surfaces. C: Properdin stabilizes the alternative convertases. D: C1 inhibitor acts on C1r and C1s.

questions.stem: The lectin pathway can be triggered by how many circulating pattern recognition receptors, and which are they?

options.A: 4 different pattern recognition receptors: three mannose-binding lectins and one ficolin
options.B: 3 different pattern recognition receptors: mannose-binding lectin, C1q and properdin
options.C: 2 different pattern recognition receptors: mannose-binding lectin and MASP-2
options.D: 4 different pattern recognition receptors: mannose-binding lectin and three ficolins
options.E: 4 different pattern recognition receptors: MASP-1, MASP-2, MASP-3 and mannose-binding lectin

questions.explanation: Lectins and ficolins act as PRRs; the lectin pathway can be triggered by any of 4 PRRs circulating in blood and extracellular fluids: MBL and 3 ficolins. A: It is one MBL and three ficolins. B: C1q and properdin belong to other pathways. C: MASP-2 is a protease, not a recognition receptor. E: MASPs are the associated serine proteases.

questions.stem: Which pair gives the PAMP examples used in the lecture with the correct organism group?

options.A: LPS of Gram-positive bacteria and lipoteichoic acid of Gram-negative bacteria
options.B: LPS of Gram-negative bacteria and lipoteichoic acid of Gram-positive bacteria
options.C: Mannose of Gram-negative bacteria and LPS of Gram-positive bacteria
options.D: Lipoteichoic acid of Gram-negative bacteria and peptidoglycan of fungi
options.E: Acetylated sugars of viruses and LPS of Gram-positive bacteria

questions.explanation: PAMPs are repeating molecular patterns on pathogens, such as LPS of Gram-negative bacteria and lipoteichoic acid of Gram-positive bacteria. A: The organism groups are swapped. C: LPS is Gram-negative. D: Lipoteichoic acid is Gram-positive. E: LPS is Gram-negative.

questions.stem: Which statement about mannose-binding lectin is correct?

options.A: It is a collectin synthesized in the liver, composed of 2 to 6 trimers (mainly 3–4)
options.B: It is a ficolin synthesized in the lung, composed of 2 to 6 trimers (mainly 3–4)
options.C: It is a collectin synthesized in the liver, composed of a hexamer of trimers with C1r and C1s
options.D: It is a collectin synthesized by neutrophils and stored in secondary granules
options.E: It is a serine protease synthesized in the liver that cleaves C4 and C2

questions.explanation: MBL is synthesized in the liver; proteins of this type are called collectins. MBL in blood is composed of 2 to 6 trimers (mainly 3–4). B: MBL is a collectin made in the liver; lung synthesis applies to M-ficolin. C: That describes the C1 complex. D: That describes properdin. E: The protease is MASP-2.

questions.stem: How do the carbohydrate-recognition domains of MBL achieve strong binding to microbial surfaces?

options.A: High affinity of each domain but low avidity for repetitive carbohydrate structures
options.B: High affinity of each domain for a single specific peptide antigen
options.C: Low affinity of each domain but high avidity for repetitive carbohydrate structures
options.D: Covalent thioester bonding of each domain to acetylated sugars
options.E: Low affinity and low avidity, compensated by a high plasma concentration

questions.explanation: Carbohydrate-recognition domains have low affinity but high avidity for repetitive carbohydrate structures on microbial surfaces. A: It is low affinity, high avidity. B: MBL recognizes repetitive carbohydrates, not specific peptides. D: Thioester bonding is a property of C4b and C3b. E: MBL is present at low concentration, and avidity is high.

questions.stem: How does the plasma level of MBL behave?

options.A: High at baseline, with production decreased during the acute-phase response to infection
options.B: Low at baseline and unchanged during infection
options.C: Higher than the ficolins at baseline and during infection
options.D: Low at baseline, with production increased during the acute-phase response to infection
options.E: Absent at baseline and produced by lung cells during infection

questions.explanation: MBL is present at low concentration in plasma, but its production is increased in the presence of infection (acute-phase response). A: It is low and increases with infection. B: Production increases in the presence of infection. C: Ficolins are more abundant in plasma. E: MBL is present at low concentration and made by the liver.

questions.stem: Which statement about human ficolins is correct?

options.A: L- and M-ficolin are synthesized in the liver; H-ficolin is secreted by lung and blood cells; they bind acetylated sugars
options.B: L- and H-ficolin are synthesized in the lung; M-ficolin is synthesized in the liver; they bind mannose residues
options.C: L- and H-ficolin are synthesized in the liver; M-ficolin is secreted by lung and blood cells; they bind acetylated sugars
options.D: L-, H- and M-ficolin are synthesized by neutrophils; they bind oligosaccharides containing sialic acid
options.E: L- and H-ficolin are synthesized in the liver; M-ficolin is secreted by lung and blood cells; they bind antibody Fc regions

questions.explanation: L-ficolin and H-ficolin are synthesized in the liver and circulate in blood; M-ficolin is synthesized and secreted by lung and blood cells. Ficolins bind oligosaccharides containing acetylated sugars. A: M-ficolin is the one made by lung and blood cells. B: Sites are swapped, and ficolins bind acetylated sugars. D: Sites are liver, lung and blood cells; the ligand is acetylated sugars. E: Ficolins bind oligosaccharides containing acetylated sugars.

questions.stem: MBL binds a pathogen surface. Which event follows in the lectin pathway?

options.A: A conformational change in MASP-1, which cleaves C3 directly to form C3bBb
options.B: Autoactivation of C1r, which cleaves C1s to act on C4 and C2
options.C: Cleavage of factor B by MASP-2 to form the C3bBb convertase
options.D: A conformational change in MASP-3, which cleaves C2 and then C5
options.E: A conformational change in MASP-2, which cleaves C4 and then C2 to form C4b2b

questions.explanation: MBL circulates in complex with MASP-1, MASP-2 and MASP-3 as inactive zymogens. Binding causes a conformational change in MASP-2, which cleaves C4 (C4b binds the surface) and then C2, giving the C3 convertase C4b2b. A: The slide names MASP-2 cleaving C4 and C2. B: That is the classical pathway. C: Factor B is cleaved by factor D in the alternative pathway. D: MASP-2 is the enzyme, and it cleaves C4 and C2.

questions.stem: Which comparison is correct according to the lecture?

options.A: MASP-2 is closely related to factor D, and MBL is more abundant in plasma than ficolins
options.B: MASP-2 is closely related to C1r and C1s, and ficolins are more abundant in plasma than MBL
options.C: MASP-2 is closely related to C1q, and ficolins are less abundant in plasma than MBL
options.D: MASP-1 is closely related to C1q, and ficolins use a different convertase than MBL
options.E: MASP-2 is closely related to C1r and C1s, and ficolins activate through factor B rather than C4

questions.explanation: MASP-2 is closely related to C1r and C1s. The same process applies for the ficolins, which are more abundant in plasma. A: MASP-2 resembles C1r/C1s, and ficolins are more abundant. C: C1q is the recognition protein; ficolins are more abundant. D: Ficolins follow the same process as MBL. E: Ficolins use the same process (C4, C2).

questions.stem: Which statement about the alternative pathway is correct?

options.A: It was the second to be discovered and does not involve the early complement components
options.B: It was the first to be discovered and does not involve the early complement components
options.C: It was the second to be discovered and starts with C1q binding to antibody
options.D: It was the last to be discovered and depends on MASP-2 cleaving C4
options.E: It was the second to be discovered and uses C4b2b as its convertase

questions.explanation: The alternative pathway was the second to be discovered after the classical pathway and does not involve early complement components. B: The classical pathway was discovered first. C: That is the classical pathway. D: It was second, and MASP-2 belongs to the lectin pathway. E: Its convertases are C3bBb and C3(H2O)Bb.

questions.stem: By which two routes is the alternative pathway activated?

options.A: C3b generated by other pathways (amplification loop) and tickover, the spontaneous cleavage of C4 by C1s
options.B: C3b from other pathways (amplification loop) and tickover, spontaneous hydrolysis of the C3 thioester bond
options.C: Antibody bound to pathogen and tickover, the spontaneous hydrolysis of the thioester bond in C3
options.D: Binding of MBL to mannose and binding of properdin to factor D
options.E: C5b deposition on the membrane and spontaneous polymerization of C9

questions.explanation: Activation occurs when C3b generated by other pathways feeds the amplification loop, or by tickover: spontaneous hydrolysis of the thioester bond in C3 to form C3(H2O). A: Tickover is hydrolysis of the thioester in C3 to C3(H2O). C: Antibody binding initiates the classical pathway. D: Not the routes described. E: These are late steps.

questions.stem: A small fraction of C3 is spontaneously cleaved to C3b without the presence of the microbe. What is the fate of this C3b?

options.A: With no infection it binds host membranes and activates complement; with a pathogen it is hydrolyzed
options.B: With no infection it accumulates in plasma as a stable convertase; with a pathogen it is inactivated by properdin
options.C: With or without infection it requires antibody before it can bind a membrane
options.D: With no infection it is converted back to C3 by factor D; with a pathogen it is cleaved by C1s
options.E: With no infection it is hydrolyzed and resolved; with a pathogen it binds the membrane and activates complement

questions.explanation: The alternative pathway can be spontaneously activated. C3b becomes hydrolyzed and is resolved if there is no infection; if there is a pathogen, C3b binds its membrane, leading to complement activation. A: The outcomes are reversed. B: The fluid-phase convertases are short-lived and properdin stabilizes them. C: The alternative pathway is antibody-independent. D: Factor D cleaves factor B, and C1s is classical.

questions.stem: In the alternative pathway, which sequence produces the C3 convertase?

options.A: Factor D binds C3b and is cleaved by factor B, giving C3bDb
options.B: Factor B binds C4b and is cleaved by C1s, giving C4bBb
options.C: Factor B binds C3b and is cleaved by factor D, giving C3bBb
options.D: Factor B binds C3a and is cleaved by properdin, giving C3aBb
options.E: Factor B binds C3b and is cleaved by MASP-2, giving C3bBa

questions.explanation: C3b binds factor B, which is cleaved by factor D, forming C3bBb. The unique convertases C3bBb and C3(H2O)Bb are short-lived. A: Factor B binds and factor D cleaves it. B: C4b and C1s are classical components. D: C3b is the binding partner and properdin only stabilizes. E: Factor D is the protease, and Bb remains bound.

questions.stem: Which complex is the C5 convertase of the alternative pathway, and what are its products?

options.A: C3bBb; C5a and C5b
options.B: C4b2b; C3a and C3b
options.C: C3(H2O)Bb; C5a and C5b
options.D: C3bBbC3b; C5a and C5b
options.E: C5b678; C9 polymers

questions.explanation: C3bBb cleaves C3 rapidly; binding of another C3b gives C3bBbC3b, the C5 convertase, which cleaves C5 into C5a and C5b. A: C3bBb is the C3 convertase; adding another C3b gives the C5 convertase. B: That is the classical/lectin C3 convertase. C: That is the fluid-phase C3 convertase. E: That is the assembling MAC, not a convertase.

questions.stem: C3b has two effector roles on the microbial surface. Which pair is correct?

options.A: It acts as an opsonin, and it joins the C3 convertase to form the C5 convertase
options.B: It acts as an opsonin, and it polymerizes to form the membrane pore
options.C: It acts as an anaphylatoxin, and it joins the C3 convertase to form the C5 convertase
options.D: It acts as a chemoattractant for neutrophils, and it inhibits C9 association with C5b-8
options.E: It acts as an opsonin, and it dissociates C1r and C1s from C1q

questions.explanation: C3b binds covalently to microbial surfaces and acts as an opsonin (phagocytosis of coated pathogens). It can also bind the C3 convertase of the classical and lectin pathways, forming the C5 convertase. B: C9 polymerizes to form the pore. C: The inflammatory small fragments are C3a, C4a and C5a. D: Inhibiting C9 association is the role of CD59. E: That is C1 inhibitor.

questions.stem: When the C5 convertase cleaves C5, how are the products described?

options.A: C5b is highly inflammatory; C5a interacts with other subunits to form the MAC
options.B: C5a is the main opsonin; C5b is released as an anaphylatoxin
options.C: C5a stabilizes the C3 convertase; C5b is the main effector molecule
options.D: C5a is highly inflammatory; C5b interacts with other subunits to form the MAC
options.E: C5a inhibits MAC formation; C5b binds factor B

questions.explanation: C5 convertase cleaves C5 into the highly inflammatory C5a and C5b, which interacts with other subunits to form the MAC, a pore in the cell membrane causing lysis. A: The roles are reversed. B: The opsonin is C3b. C: Properdin stabilizes the convertase and C3b is the main effector. E: CD59 inhibits MAC formation, and factor B binds C3b.

questions.stem: How does the membrane attack complex kill, in the lecture's description of the late steps?

options.A: C5b polymerizes where C9 has bound, forming a pore for ions and water, with osmotic swelling and rupture
options.B: C9 polymerizes where C3b has bound, forming a pore for proteins, with apoptosis of the cell
options.C: C6 polymerizes where C5b has bound, forming a channel that delivers granzymes into the cell
options.D: C9 polymerizes where C5b has bound, sealing the membrane and trapping the pathogen for phagocytosis
options.E: C9 polymerizes where C5b has bound, forming a pore for ions and water, with osmotic swelling and rupture

questions.explanation: C9 polymerizes at the site where C5b has bound, forming a pore in the plasma membrane (channels for ions and water), leading to osmotic swelling and rupture. A: C9 is the component that polymerizes. B: The site is C5b and death is by osmotic rupture. C: Granzymes belong to NK killing; C9 polymerizes. D: It creates a pore, not a seal.

questions.stem: Which proteins cluster in the pathogen membrane to form the MAC, and against which organisms is it said to be especially useful?

options.A: C5a and C6 to C9; Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
options.B: C5b and C6 to C9; Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
options.C: C3b and C5 to C9; Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae
options.D: C5b and C6 to C9; Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes
options.E: C4b, C2b and C9; Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae

questions.explanation: Proteins C5b and C6–C9 cluster in the pathogen's membrane and ultimately kill it; the MAC is useful against Neisseria meningitidis and gonorrhoeae. A: C5b, not C5a, starts the MAC. C: C3b is not part of the MAC, and the organisms named are Neisseria. D: The slide names Neisseria species. E: C4b2b is the C3 convertase.

questions.stem: In the complement activation overview, which fragments are assigned to inflammation, which to opsonization and phagocytosis, and what lyses the microbe?

options.A: C3b and C5b to inflammation; C3a to opsonization and phagocytosis; the MAC lyses the microbe
options.B: C3a and C5a to opsonization and phagocytosis; C3b to inflammation; C5a lyses the microbe
options.C: C3a and C5a to inflammation; C3b to opsonization and phagocytosis; the MAC lyses the microbe
options.D: C4a and C2b to inflammation; C5b to opsonization and phagocytosis; C3b lyses the microbe
options.E: C3a and C5a to inflammation; C5b to opsonization and phagocytosis; C9 monomers lyse the microbe

questions.explanation: Effector functions: C3a and C5a induce inflammation, C3b opsonizes for phagocytosis, and the MAC lyses the microbe. A: The a-fragments are inflammatory and C3b is the opsonin. B: The roles are swapped. D: C3b is the opsonin, and lysis is by the MAC. E: C3b is the opsonin, and lysis needs the assembled MAC.

questions.stem: Regarding regulation, which statement is NOT consistent with the lecture?

options.A: Regulators are expressed on infected cells and are absent from normal host cells
options.B: Complement must be controlled so that it is activated on pathogens or damaged host cells
options.C: Once a cell is infected, the regulatory molecules on its surface become absent
options.D: Complement can be activated by dying cells, leading to their phagocytosis
options.E: Clearing dying cells avoids autoimmune responses to released intracellular contents

questions.explanation: Regulators are expressed on the surface of normal cells; once a cell is infected they become absent, leading to complement activation. Dying cells can also activate complement so they are phagocytosed, avoiding autoimmune responses. B: Stated on the slide. C: Stated on the slide. D: Stated on the slide. E: Stated on the slide.

questions.stem: Which statement about properdin (factor P) is correct?

options.A: It is a negative regulator of complement, accelerating the decay of C3bBb and C3(H2O)Bb
options.B: It is the positive regulator of complement, stabilizing the classical convertase C4b2b
options.C: It is a cofactor for factor I in the cleavage and inactivation of C3b
options.D: It is the positive regulator of complement, stabilizing C3bBb and C3(H2O)Bb
options.E: It is the positive regulator of complement, promoting C9 association with C5b-8

questions.explanation: Properdin is the only positive regulator of complement: C3bBb and C3(H2O)Bb are stabilized by binding this plasma protein. A: Decay acceleration is done by DAF, CFH or CR1. B: It stabilizes the alternative pathway convertases. C: That is MCP, CFH or CR1. E: It acts on the alternative C3 convertases.

questions.stem: Where does properdin come from?

options.A: Hepatocytes, which secrete it during the acute-phase response
options.B: Neutrophils, which store it in azurophilic granules and release it continuously while at rest
options.C: Lung and blood cells, which secrete it into the circulation
options.D: Macrophages, which express it on their surface as a complement receptor
options.E: Neutrophils, which store it in secondary granules and release it when activated by pathogens

questions.explanation: Factor P is produced by neutrophils and stored in secondary granules, released upon neutrophil activation by pathogens; it can also bind some pathogen membranes, directing the alternative pathway. A: Hepatic acute-phase production was described for MBL. B: The slide says secondary granules and release on activation. C: That describes M-ficolin. D: It is a plasma protein released by neutrophils.

questions.stem: What is distinctive about C1 esterase inhibitor?

options.A: It is the serine protease inhibitor that dissociates activated C1r and C1s from C1q and blocks spontaneous C1 activation
options.B: It is the serine protease inhibitor that dissociates C4b from C2b in the convertase and blocks spontaneous C3 hydrolysis
options.C: It is a membrane protein that accelerates the dissociation of C3bBb on host cells
options.D: It is a cofactor for CFI-mediated cleavage and inactivation of C3b or C4b
options.E: It is a membrane protein that inhibits C9 association with C5b-8

questions.explanation: C1INH is the only serine protease inhibitor known to dissociate activated C1r and C1s from C1q, limiting the time the complex is active; it also blocks spontaneous activation of C1 by plasma proteases. B: Its targets are C1r and C1s. C: That is DAF. D: That is MCP (or CFH, CR1). E: That is CD59.

questions.stem: Match the negative regulators with their mechanism.

options.A: DAF: cofactor for CFI cleavage of C3b; MCP: decay acceleration of C3 convertases; CD59: blocks C9 association with C5b-8
options.B: DAF: blocks C9 association with C5b-8; MCP: cofactor for CFI cleavage of C3b; CD59: decay acceleration of C3 convertases
options.C: DAF: decay acceleration of C3 convertases; MCP: cofactor for CFI cleavage of C3b; CD59: blocks C9 association with C5b-8
options.D: DAF: decay acceleration of C3 convertases; MCP: blocks C9 association with C5b-8; CD59: cofactor for CFI cleavage of C3b
options.E: DAF: dissociates C1r and C1s from C1q; MCP: stabilizes C3bBb; CD59: cofactor for CFI cleavage of C4b

questions.explanation: Decay-accelerating activity: DAF (or CFH, CR1) destabilizes C3 convertases. Cofactor activity: MCP (or CFH, CR1) binds C3b as cofactor for CFI-mediated cleavage. CD59 inhibits C9 association with C5b-8, preventing MAC formation. A: DAF and MCP are swapped. B: DAF and CD59 are swapped. D: MCP and CD59 are swapped. E: These are the actions of C1INH and properdin, and CD59 blocks MAC formation.

questions.stem: Which inheritance pattern statement is correct for complement deficiencies?

options.A: Most are autosomal recessive; properdin deficiency is autosomal dominant and C1 inhibitor deficiency is X-linked recessive
options.B: Most are autosomal recessive; properdin deficiency is X-linked recessive and C1 inhibitor deficiency is autosomal dominant
options.C: Most are autosomal dominant; properdin deficiency is X-linked recessive and C1 inhibitor deficiency is autosomal recessive
options.D: Most are X-linked recessive; properdin deficiency is autosomal recessive and C1 inhibitor deficiency is autosomal dominant
options.E: Most are autosomal recessive; MBL deficiency is X-linked recessive and DAF deficiency is autosomal dominant

questions.explanation: All complement deficiencies are autosomal recessive except properdin deficiency (X-linked recessive) and C1INH deficiency (autosomal dominant). A: The two exceptions are swapped. C: The rule is autosomal recessive, and C1INH deficiency is dominant. D: The rule is autosomal recessive, and properdin is the X-linked one. E: The exceptions are properdin and C1INH.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old has repeated respiratory infections with common extracellular bacteria. Work-up shows an isolated defect of the lectin pathway. Which deficiency fits, and why is early childhood the vulnerable period?

options.A: MBL or MASP-2 deficiency; adaptive immunity is not yet fully developed in early childhood
options.B: MBL or MASP-2 deficiency; maternal antibodies block the classical pathway in early childhood
options.C: Properdin deficiency; adaptive immunity is not yet fully developed
options.D: C2 or C4 deficiency; immune complexes are cleared poorly
options.E: C5–C9 deficiency; the MAC cannot form on encapsulated bacteria

questions.explanation: Deficiency of MASP-2 or MBL alters the lectin pathway and increases susceptibility to respiratory infections by common extracellular bacteria during early childhood, when adaptive immunity is not fully developed. B: The reason given is immature adaptive immunity. C: Properdin deficiency affects the alternative pathway and predisposes to Neisseria meningitidis. D: That combination is linked to systemic lupus. E: Terminal deficiencies give recurrent Neisseria infections.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy develops bacterial meningitis due to Neisseria meningitidis; a maternal uncle had the same infection. Deficiency of which alternative pathway protein fits the inheritance and the lecture?

options.A: Factor D deficiency
options.B: Properdin deficiency
options.C: C1 inhibitor deficiency
options.D: MASP-2 deficiency
options.E: C4 deficiency

questions.explanation: Properdin (factor P) deficiency is X-linked recessive and makes patients susceptible to Neisseria meningitidis, the main agent of bacterial meningitis. A: Not discussed as a disease; the X-linked deficiency linked to N. meningitidis is properdin. C: Autosomal dominant, causing hereditary angioneurotic edema. D: Lectin pathway defect with early-childhood respiratory infections. E: Early classical defect linked to systemic lupus.

questions.stem: Why do patients deficient in early classical components (especially C1q, C1r, C1s and C4, or C2) develop systemic lupus erythematosus, according to the lecture?

options.A: Unregulated MAC formation on red cells
options.B: Excess C2 kinin generation
options.C: Loss of properdin stabilization
options.D: Defective clearance of immune complexes
options.E: Failure of C9 polymerization

questions.explanation: Deficiency of early classical components (C1q, C1r, C1s and C4; C2 or C4) leads to SLE because of defective clearance of immune complexes. A: That is the mechanism in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. B: That occurs in C1 inhibitor deficiency. C: Properdin deficiency predisposes to Neisseria infection. E: That would impair the MAC and predispose to Neisseria.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of skin swelling, abdominal pain, vomiting and one episode of laryngeal edema. Her father had similar attacks. Which mechanism and treatment match the lecture?

options.A: C1 inhibitor deficiency with massive breakdown of C3 and C5 and generation of C5a; prophylactic antibiotics
options.B: DAF deficiency with unregulated complement on red cells; recombinant C1INH
options.C: C1 inhibitor deficiency with massive breakdown of C4 and C2 and generation of C2 kinin; recombinant C1INH
options.D: Properdin deficiency with unstable C3bBb; immunosuppressors
options.E: C1q deficiency with defective immune complex clearance; recombinant C1q

questions.explanation: Hereditary angioneurotic edema is autosomal dominant C1 inhibitor deficiency (increased complement activation): edema of skin, possible asphyxiation from laryngeal edema, GI symptoms, due to massive breakdown of C4 and C2 with products such as C2 kinin. Treatment: recombinant C1INH. A: The slide names C4 and C2 breakdown, with C2 kinin; treatment is recombinant C1INH. B: DAF deficiency causes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. D: Properdin deficiency causes Neisseria infections. E: C1q deficiency is linked to lupus, not angioedema.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man reports very dark urine in the morning, fatigue, easy bruising and a recent venous thrombosis. He has chronic hemolytic anemia. Which mechanism does the lecture give?

options.A: Inherited germline mutation in hepatocytes causing C1 inhibitor deficiency and unregulated C1 activity
options.B: Acquired somatic mutation in hematopoietic stem cells causing properdin deficiency and unstable alternative convertases on red cells
options.C: Inherited deficiency of C5–C9 causing failure of MAC formation on red cells
options.D: Acquired autoantibody against C1q causing consumption of C3 and C4
options.E: Acquired somatic mutation in hematopoietic stem cells causing DAF deficiency and unregulated complement on red cells

questions.explanation: This is paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria: inherited DAF deficiency is uncommon, but an acquired somatic mutation in hematopoietic stem cells causes chronic hemolytic anemia from unregulated complement activation on red cells, thrombosis and impaired bone marrow function, with very dark urine in the morning. A: That is hereditary angioneurotic edema. B: The deficient regulator is DAF. C: In PNH, complement activity on red cells is excessive. D: Not the mechanism described.

questions.stem: Besides destruction of red blood cells, which two features characterize paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria in the lecture?

options.A: Thrombosis and impaired bone marrow function
options.B: Thrombosis and laryngeal edema
options.C: Recurrent Neisseria infections and impaired bone marrow function
options.D: Systemic lupus and impaired clearance of immune complexes
options.E: Angioedema and C2 kinin generation

questions.explanation: PNH is characterized by destruction of red blood cells, blood clots (thrombosis) and impaired bone marrow function. B: Laryngeal edema belongs to C1 inhibitor deficiency. C: Neisseria infections are linked to properdin and terminal deficiencies. D: These are linked to early classical deficiencies. E: These belong to hereditary angioneurotic edema.

questions.stem: A patient with active systemic lupus has low complement levels although she has no inherited deficiency. How does the lecture explain this, and which proteins are low?

options.A: Acquired deficiency: the autoimmune condition blocks hepatic synthesis of complement proteins; C5 and C9
options.B: Inherited deficiency unmasked by infection; C1q and properdin
options.C: Acquired deficiency: the autoimmune condition causes complement proteins to get used up; C3 and C4
options.D: Acquired deficiency: autoantibodies stabilize the C3 convertase; factor B and factor D
options.E: Acquired deficiency: loss of DAF from red cells; C3 and C4

questions.explanation: Complement deficiency may be inherited (most autosomal recessive) or acquired: severe infection or an autoimmune condition such as SLE causes complement proteins to get used up, with C3 and C4 deficiency. A: The mechanism is consumption, and the proteins named are C3 and C4. B: The slide describes acquired consumption of C3 and C4. D: Not the mechanism described. E: DAF loss is the PNH mechanism.

questions.stem: Compare early (C1–C4) with terminal (C5–C9) complement deficiencies.

options.A: Early: impaired MAC formation with recurrent Neisseria infections; terminal: severe recurrent pyogenic infections and SLE
options.B: Early: recurrent Neisseria infections and SLE; terminal: hereditary angioedema
options.C: Early: severe recurrent viral infections; terminal: paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
options.D: Early: severe recurrent pyogenic infections; terminal: SLE from immune complex deposition
options.E: Early: severe recurrent pyogenic infections and SLE; terminal: impaired MAC formation with recurrent Neisseria infections

questions.explanation: Early deficiencies (C1–C4) raise the risk of severe, recurrent pyogenic infections and autoimmune manifestations (SLE). Terminal deficiencies (C5–C9) impair MAC formation, giving recurrent Neisseria infections (meningitis or gonorrhea). A: The two groups are swapped. B: Angioedema is C1 inhibitor deficiency, and Neisseria belongs to terminal deficiencies. C: Early deficiencies give pyogenic infections and PNH is DAF deficiency. D: SLE belongs to early deficiencies.

questions.stem: Which blood tests are listed for diagnosing a complement deficiency?

options.A: Overall complement activity (CH50 or CH100) and flow cytometry for CD59 and DAF
options.B: Overall complement activity (CH50 or CH100) and specific protein levels (C3 or C4)
options.C: Antinuclear antibody titer and specific protein levels (C3 or C4)
options.D: Overall complement activity (AH50) and properdin gene sequencing
options.E: C1 inhibitor function assay and bone marrow biopsy

questions.explanation: Diagnosis is by blood analysis: overall complement activity (CH50 or CH100) and specific protein levels (C3 or C4). A: Not listed on the slide. C: Not listed as a complement test. D: Not listed on the slide. E: Not listed on the slide.

questions.stem: How does treatment differ between an underactive and an overactive complement response?

options.A: Underactive: immunosuppressors; overactive: precautionary prophylactic antibiotics; a deficient protein such as C1INH can also be supplemented
options.B: Underactive: recombinant C1INH; overactive: prophylactic antibiotics; a deficient protein such as properdin can also be supplemented
options.C: Underactive: plasma exchange; overactive: immunosuppressors; deficient proteins cannot be supplemented
options.D: Underactive: precautionary prophylactic antibiotics; overactive: immunosuppressors; a deficient protein such as C1INH can also be supplemented
options.E: Underactive: prophylactic antibiotics; overactive: antihistamines; a deficient protein such as C3 can also be supplemented

questions.explanation: Underactive response: treat infections and take precautions with prophylactic antibiotics. Overactive/autoimmune manifestations: immunosuppressors. A deficient protein can also be supplemented, such as C1INH. A: The two are swapped. B: C1INH is the supplementation example, used for C1INH deficiency. C: Supplementation is possible, and plasma exchange is not listed. E: The slide lists immunosuppressors and C1INH.

questions.stem: Each of the following describes the complement proteins in the take-home messages EXCEPT:

options.A: They are circulating proteins synthesized by the liver
options.B: They act as proteases and cleave one another in cascade
options.C: They bind to pathogens as well as immune complexes
options.D: They participate in humoral immunity and alert phagocytes of the innate system
options.E: They are synthesized by plasma cells and act as receptors on lymphocytes

questions.explanation: Complement is a group of circulating proteins that are synthesized by the liver, participate in humoral immunity, act as proteases cleaving one another in cascade, bind pathogens and immune complexes, and alert phagocytes. A: Stated in the take-home messages. B: Stated in the take-home messages. C: Stated in the take-home messages. D: Stated in the take-home messages.

questions.stem: Which inflammatory complement subunits cause vascular changes, according to the list of complement functions?

options.A: C3b, C4b and C5b
options.B: C3a, C4a and C5a
options.C: C3a, C5a and C9
options.D: C2b, C3b and C5a
options.E: C1q, C3a and C5b

questions.explanation: Functions include opsonization, clearance of immune complexes and cellular debris, chemotaxis of neutrophils, direct cytolysis through the MAC, and vascular changes caused by the inflammatory subunits C3a, C4a and C5a. A: The b-fragments bind surfaces (opsonization, convertases, MAC). C: C9 forms the pore. D: Only C5a of these is listed. E: C1q is the recognition protein and C5b starts the MAC.

questions.stem: In the summary table of activation pathways, what does each pathway detect?

options.A: Classical: surfaces with mannose; alternative: surfaces not protected by complement inhibitors; lectin: surfaces with bound IgG or IgM
options.B: Classical: surfaces with bound IgG or IgM; alternative: surfaces with mannose; lectin: surfaces not protected by complement inhibitors
options.C: Classical: surfaces with bound IgA or IgE; alternative: surfaces coated with properdin; lectin: surfaces with acetylated lipids
options.D: Classical: surfaces with bound IgG or IgM; alternative: surfaces not protected by complement inhibitors; lectin: surfaces with mannose
options.E: Classical: surfaces not protected by complement inhibitors; alternative: surfaces with bound IgG or IgM; lectin: surfaces with mannose

questions.explanation: Table: classical detects surfaces with bound antibodies (IgG and IgM); alternative detects surfaces not protected by complement inhibitors; lectin detects surfaces with mannose. A: Classical and lectin are swapped. B: Alternative and lectin are swapped. C: The table lists IgG and IgM, unprotected surfaces, and mannose. E: Classical and alternative are swapped.
